::: {.lx-sec-h}
## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a18-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Inventory</dt><dd>Count first, by scope: what the city burns (scope 1), the grid electricity it uses (scope 2) and the losses on the wires (scope 3).</dd>
<dt>Curve</dt><dd>Each bar is one measure alone: its width the tonnes it avoids, its height the cost per tonne. Below zero it saves more than it costs.</dd>
<dt>Tests</dt><dd>A plan also needs money up front, room at each substation on the coldest morning, and a fair answer to who gains and who pays.</dd>
<dt>Where it misleads</dt><dd>Measures overlap and compete, order and lock-in matter, the baseline and prices move the bars, and a saving on paper does not install itself.</dd>
<dt>Who decides</dt><dd>The city counts and adopts; the utility runs programmes and supply; the state regulator approves the utility's parts; owners make most choices.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>A city's inventory under the GPC</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **The standard.** The Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Emission Inventories (GPC), by WRI, C40 Cities and ICLEI, final version December 2014.
- **Scopes** (Table 3.2, p. 31). Scope 1: sources inside the city boundary. Scope 2: grid-supplied electricity, heat, steam or cooling used inside it. Scope 3: other emissions outside the boundary caused by activities inside it.
- **Rooftop solar.** Power from panels used where they stand is not grid-supplied, so Prairie City's scope 2 leaves it out: the homes' and businesses' electricity less their rooftop share.
- **Two reporting levels** (Box 4.1, p. 36). BASIC: scopes 1 and 2 of stationary energy and transport, and waste. BASIC+ adds industrial processes (IPPU), agriculture and land, trips across the boundary, and losses on the wires.
- **Prairie City's subtotals.** Scopes 1 and 2: 2,701,349 t. With the losses (scope 3): 2,766,098 t, the inventory the targets use.
- **Not BASIC or BASIC+.** They count CO₂ only (the GPC asks for seven gases, p. 30), leave out waste and do not split out the fertilizer plant's feedstock: teaching subtotals, not GPC reporting totals.
- **Farm machinery.** Tractors and other farm machinery go under stationary energy, agriculture (Table 6.5, p. 62), not transport.
- **Feedstock.** Fossil fuel used as a feedstock, like the gas the fertilizer plant turns into hydrogen, goes under IPPU (p. 56). This data does not split it from the gas the plant burns.
- **Each year.** The GPC recommends updating the inventory every year to track progress (p. 12).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>How one bar is priced</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

$$\text{cost per tonne} = \frac{\text{extra capital} \times \mathrm{CRF} + \text{extra upkeep} + \text{change in energy bills}}{\text{tonnes of CO}_2\text{ avoided a year}}, \qquad \mathrm{CRF} = \frac{r}{1-(1+r)^{-n}}$$

- **Symbols.** $r$ is the real discount rate (4% a year); $n$ the item's life in years; CRF the [capital recovery factor]{.lx-term term="capital-recovery-factor"}, which spreads an up-front cost into equal yearly payments. Money in 2025 dollars, a year.
- **Heat-pump water heaters.** The heat pump costs $810 more than a new electric heater in 2022 dollars, $884.58 in 2025 dollars. By 2035, 20,777 homes heated with electricity replace theirs: $18.4M up front.
- **A year.** That capital × CRF (4%, 15.1 years) = $1,645,017. The homes save 46,781 MWh, $6,755,228 at 14.44¢ per kWh, and avoid 46,781 × 0.391 × 1.05 = 19,206 t.
- **The bar.** (1,645,017 − 6,755,228) ÷ 19,206 = −$266 per t: it saves more than it costs.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>From a curve to a planning model</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **A curve ranks measures one at a time.** A planning model chooses them together: each measure's level is a decision between zero and its potential.
- **Rules a curve cannot hold.** The heat balance links weatherization and heat pumps; each district's highest hour must stay under its substation limit; the up-front money must fit a budget; the cut must reach the target.
- **The goal.** The least net annual cost that meets every rule.
- **Overlaps.** A heat pump in a weatherized home saves less. A planning model must represent such overlaps explicitly; <span class="a18-ref" data-code="M12"><a href="m12-city-model.html">M12</a></span> introduces suitable formulations.
- **Next.** <span class="a18-ref" data-code="M12"><a href="m12-city-model.html">M12</a></span> builds such a city energy hub, <span class="a18-ref" data-code="SB3"><a href="sb3-city-planner.html">SB3</a></span> lets you run one, and <span class="a18-ref" data-code="C3"><a href="c3-prairie-city-2040.html">C3</a></span> asks for Prairie City's 2040 plan.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Transport, 31% of the inventory, the industrial park and the grid's own plan: none has a bar here. The grid's change still counts toward the target (step 8).</li>
<li>Rebound, comfort, health and the soft costs of taking part.</li>
<li>How lower sales move rates for every customer, and energy burden: <span class="a18-ref" data-code="A13"><a href="a13-fairness-jobs.html">A13</a></span>.</li>
<li>The cost of a bigger substation, and furnace fans at the peak hour.</li>
<li>Cooling when a heat pump replaces an air conditioner: counted as unchanged.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a18-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="grid" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A city decides its own electricity emissions.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Prairie City's 1,282,744 t of scope 2 follow the regional grid's rate. In step 8 the much cleaner grid alone cuts 830,547 t a year of scope 2 and the losses' scope 3.</p><p>Cities influence demand, and some run their own utility, as Los Angeles does; the regional supply's emissions involve utilities, markets and public policy.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="negative" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A measure below zero on the curve will happen by itself, because it saves money.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Its cost leaves out the time and hassle of taking part, and a landlord who pays gets none of a tenant's savings. Programmes, rules and financing exist for that gap.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="add" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Adding up the bars you pick gives your plan's cut.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Alone, the six bars add to 164,692 t; together they cut 150,854 t. Heat pumps and condensing furnaces compete for the same furnaces, and weatherized homes need less heat.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="solar" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “New rooftop solar lowers Prairie City's highest hour of the year.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth, here. Each district's highest hour is 07:00 on the cold design day, before the sun is up enough: 60 MW of new panels lower it by under 0.1 MW.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a18">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="price" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">A measure costs $300 a year more to own and saves $100 a year of energy. It avoids 2 t of CO₂ a year. What is its cost per tonne?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$100 per t</li><li data-value="b">$150 per t</li><li data-value="c">−$100 per t</li><li data-value="d">$200 per t</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$100 per t: (300 − 100) ÷ 2. The energy saved is subtracted before dividing.</p><p>$150 per t forgets the saving; −$100 per t gets the sign of the saving wrong.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p><b>New York City.</b> Over two thirds of the city's greenhouse-gas emissions are attributed to buildings. Local Law 97 of 2019 sets emissions limits for most buildings over 25,000 square feet from 2024, with stricter limits from 2030.</p>
<p>For 2024, the first compliance year, about 95% of the 19,963 properties required to report filed (NYC Department of Buildings, 2026).</p>
<p><b>Los Angeles.</b> In 2016 and 2017 the City Council passed motions directing its city-owned utility, LADWP, to study a 100% renewable power system; NREL ran the LA100 study (March 2021).</p>
<p>Peak demand grows in all its projections, but more slowly than annual electricity use (LA100 executive summary, p. 20).</p>
<p class="lx-hint">Los Angeles peaks on hot afternoons. In a cold city, heat pumps can put the peak on the coldest morning, as step 5 showed.</p>
</div>
```
